speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an important international event that will take place this summer in Montreal, and I am referring to the 19th World Congress of the International Union of Forestry Organizations.
From August 5 to 11, scientists from 105 countries, representing nearly 700 affiliated organizations, will be meeting in Montreal. Since the 19th Congress will conclude IUFRO's first 100 years, this will be an opportunity for delegates to examine where forestry science is heading on the eve of IUFRO's next century.
The Congress will also be our chance to show others the abundance and variety of our forests as well as the technology that has made Canada one of the foremost countries in this field.
Canada is a full-fledged member of the world forestry community, and Canadians involved in forestry are very much aware of the need for international exchanges. The Canadian forestry industry, recognizing its responsibility for managing an invaluable resource, has therefore joined forces to organize this Congress.
Mr. Speaker, we extend a cordial welcome to all participants.

Mr. Speaker, May 6 to 12 marks this year's celebration of National Forest Week. The 1990 theme will be "Living Forest -Giving Forest ".
We are all becoming more conscious of the rich resources that we have at our disposal. At the present time approximately one million Canadian workers depend on the forest industry.
National Forest Week gives all Canadians a chance to reflect on how the forest touches our lives. Wouldn't it be great if in the next few months the Federal-provincial Resource Development Agreements were renewed. These agreements are essential to the viability of our forests if we are to achieve some of our environmental objectives as well as maintain forestry's economic contribution regionally and nationally.

All Canadians are environmentally conscious and want to help save the environment, including our forests. Forests have much to offer us, and it is therefore our duty to protect this resource.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister must know he is on a sinking ship when his political friends run for the lifeboats. When the four western premiers arrived in Portage la Prairie yesterday for their annual conference they made it very clear that they are together on at least one thing. None of them are veiy happy with the federal government these days.
Whatever the topic-the GST, farm aid, the cut in funding for health and post-secondary education, high interest rates or the failure to re-negotiate federal-

May 7, 1990
provincial agreements on tourism, forestry or northern developments-the message is the same. The Conservatives in Ottawa are putting the screws to the west, and the west will not take it much longer.
Never mind that three of the four premiers are Conservatives themselves and the fourth is a closet Tory. Never mind that they all supported the Conservative platform in the last election. The federal Conservatives are now at a record low in the polls and it seems that these days the four western premiers cannot backpeddle fast enough to get away from their federal counterparts.
All the same, Mr. Speaker, I caution the voters in western Canada to remember that provincial Conservatives are Conservatives too, no matter what they complain about with regard to federal Conservatives. They are all the same, they do the same, they act the same, they just speak with different mouths.

Mr. Speaker, five years ago, the government proposed a plan for sound economic management and better management of government operations.
I rise in the House today to pay tribute to the work done by employees of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Hear, hear!

At a time of budgetary restrictions when sound and efficient management is needed, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been able to meet the government's objectives.
Mr. Speaker, for the first time in ten years, the CMHC's mortgage insurance fund has succeeded in meeting its obligations without government assistance.
In 1989 alone, the CMHC deposited more than $62 million in the Treasury, in addition to providing Canadians with 627,000 housing units.
Mr. Speaker, in many respects the CMHC is indeed the efficient performer referred to by the Auditor General of Canada.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, forestry employs 8 per cent of all Canadians and generates over $40 billion annually. Forestry is the lifeblood of many single industry towns in our country.
Despite these facts, this government neglects Canada's chief industry. The 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber coupled with the strong Canadian dollar and high interest rates are crippling this industry in Canada and for small-town Canada. To date seven provincial forest agreements have been allowed to lapse.
But most important, the government fails to recognize that the key element to any environmental plan is our forests. In fact, its new framework for discussion on the environment devotes only one half page to the protection of forests in Canada.
As Dr. James Kayll, the renowned forester from Lakehead University in Thunder Bay says: "You can't discuss the environment without discussing trees and you can't discuss trees without discussing the environment". It is time we started to do both.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, restraint in government expenditures will reduce the burden on monetary policy in fighting inflation and create greater scope for lower interest rates and a lower dollar.
To date considerable progress has been made. Spending restraint has provided the largest share of our deficit reduction efforts. It has involved a number of necessary decisions, which are always difficult and sometimes unpopular.
We, as a government, must have continuing action to control expenditures. In our fiscal situation the government can ill afford examples to the contrary, such as the reported expenses at Ports Canada.
May 7, 1990

Indeed, we bear a responsibility to search out and eliminate wasteful spending, improve our efficiency and ensure the best value for the taxpayers' dollars.
Our government must continue to evaluate all government expenditures in this context. The end result is much-needed latitude for our monetary policy in curbing inflation.
Only at this time can Canadians, and in particular our exports, have the opportunity to benefit from lower interest rates and a lower Canadian dollar.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, the spring lobster season is now one week old. Prices during the week were $1.75 for market lobsters and $1.25 for canner lobsters. These are the lowest season opening prices in years, but the fishermen's expenses have never stopped increasing.
People in the industry are not optimistic about the chances of the situation improving, mainly because of the large inventory currently being held by the processors. These prices are so low that many fishermen will actually lose money if they put to sea. This is the third consecutive poor season for the lobster fishermen of Prince Edward Island.
I realize that extensive new marketing schemes are being developed and that some have already been put in place, but these are plans which are expected to resolve the situation down the road. They will not solve the immediate problem.
I am asking the government to use the Fisheries Prices Support Board as an interim measure to establish prices which will allow fishermen to continue to fish in an economically viable situation.
This board is already in existence, so I ask the government to act quickly so that our fishermen will have a chance to salvage their season and the processors will continue to have a viable operation.

Mr. Speaker, since 1980, Quebecers have had the benefit of consumer
protection legislation. When they use a credit card to make a payment, interest is calculated only on the balance payable. Unfortunately, it has come to our attention that the National Bank of Canada, which agreed to observe the legislation, has decided, as a result of pressure by other banks, to charge Quebec consumers $1.5 million more because it will be applying the same policy as the rest of the federally-chartered banks.
Today I want the federal government to order the National Bank of Canada, first of all, to appear before the Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Public Administration, to find out whether it is, in fact, proceeding in this matter; and second, to find out whether it would not be preferable for the federal government to monitor the way the chartered banks are calculating and charging interest.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians from all parts of the country took time during the recent national Mental Health Week to acknowledge the contribution of all those who serve in that field. I would like to endorse those statements, albeit belatedly.
Although these remarks have been prompted, at least in part, by the extremely thoughtful, attentive care which all members of the staff at Fairview Home in Brandon have been providing to a member of my own family who has been extremely ill for several weeks, I would like, as a member of Parliament, to express what I believe is our collective appreciation to the unknown legions of Canadians who provide health care, regardless of their area of specialization, each hour of each day of each week and who all too frequently receive little or no thanks for doing so.
Canada has perhaps the best health care system in the world thanks largely to the thousands of professional and dedicated people who serve the public so faithfully.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, May 4, Latvia adopted a declaration to restore the republic's independence from the Soviet Union. The declaration states the Soviet annexation of 1940 as

May 7, 1990
Oral Questions
illegal, re-establishing portions of the 1922 constitution declaring Latvia an independent democratic republic.
The declaration also pledges an unspecified transition period to restore the republic's actual independence from the U.S.S.R., during which period it promises to abide by Soviet laws as long as those laws do not infringe on Latvian sovereignty.
All three Baltic states have now declared their independence. As a member of Parliament in a country that has never recognized the annexation of the Baltic states, it is my hope that this time it does not take as long for the two sides to come to the table.
Having just returned from the Soviet Union, it is also my hope that negotiations in peace and good faith will take precedence over economic sanctions. This is an opportunity, in the spirit of co-operation and confidence that is sweeping all of Europe, to rectify a situation that was a result of, at best, a dubious and questionable agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Today, after holding their breath for more than a year, the people of Atlantic Canada were finally given a package for the fishery that is totally inadequate, judging by the magnitude of the problem. Yet, on December 13, 1989, the Prime Minister said:
- the Government of Canada will act in respect of the Atlantic fishery with exactly the same kind of generosity and enthusiasm that we brought to resolving the problems of the prairie farmer a few years ago.
Mr. Speaker, that was a billion dollar program for only one year. The government announced today a program of $587 million over five years and one-third of that, the government has already announced, is not even new money.
Why has the government not come forward with a truly meaningful program to maintain the fishing communities of Atlantic Canada until the fish stocks recover? Why will the government not recognize that we are dealing with a truly important, valuable and renewable resource?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada announced today, in addition to a significant contribution announced some months ago, the dedication of another $426 million to deal with the crisis that has been caused in Atlantic Canada by developments in the fishing industry, particularly with regard to northern cod but also with regard to other species.
It is designed to help ensure that people who make their livelihood in that industry, who contribute to the growth of Canada in that industry, will either be able to continue in that industry with the benefit of new research and the benefit of new projects being sponsored by this government, or will be able to make adjustments to other kinds of effective economic activity as effectively as possible.
It is a significant major step clearly comparable to the action that this Government of Canada took with regard to western farmers facing an earlier but different crisis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just admitted that the government today has not announced the kind of program the Prime Minister spoke of when he talked about western farmers last December.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister talks about making adjustments, he really means phasing out. In other words, whole communities will disappear, and families will have to give up their traditional way of life.
I want to ask the minister this: How many families will have to lose their livelihood? How many communities, so far prosperous, must turn into ghost towns until the government realizes that the fisheries are a durable industry that should be promoted and not closed down? How many more Scheffervilles is the government going to give us?
Yes, how many?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whatever the government's poli-
May 7, 1990

cies or statements may contain, we can count on the Hon. Leader of the Opposition to say it just isn't enough.
The reality, Mr. Speaker, is very clear. What has been announced today is a major program designed to rebuild the fish stocks at a time when there is a significant environmental threat to the stocks that make viable our east coast fishing communities. It is a major contribution to programs that will allow the communities and the people involved in the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada to adjust constructively to these kinds of realities and, also, a significant new contribution to economic diversification in Atlantic Canada.
Earlier the Leader of the Opposition talked about the comparisons between western Canada and Atlantic Canada. He will know that there are over 165,000 farmers in western Canada. There are 60,000 fishermen in Atlantic Canada. What has been announced today is a new $426 million program to help Atlantic Canada. That amounts, in total, to $584 million being spent by the Government of Canada over this period to help ensure that we maintain a viable fishing industry and viable alternatives for people who have been working in that industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister talks of the need to rebuild the fish stocks, which problem he says is due to an environmental situation.
The Harris report identified foreign overfishing as a major contributor to the depletion of our fish stocks. Yet, all we see in the government's announcement today is that it will continue "intensive, diplomatic and political efforts" to try to resolve the problem.
This means that the Spanish and Portuguese will continue to pillage our stocks and the European community will continue to set quotas far above what these stocks can sustain.
If the government is serious about foreign overfishing, why did it not declare today Canadian jurisdiction over the nose and tail of the Grand Banks? Why did it not stand up for Canadians just once? Why did it not speak for Canadians when it had the chance to do so?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition should not be driven by his new responsibilities to abandon the reputation for seriousness that he has won over the years in this House of Commons.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He knows far better than to make accusations of that kind.
Let me make a point about conservation. The Leader of the Opposition is suggesting by the tone of that question that the conservation issue is not an important issue in this debate. If, by chance, he is quoted in Europe with regard to those views which are at variance with the facts and at variance with the reports of the Harris committee and others, he will make it far more difficult for us to carry on a campaign that has already found some success. This is a campaign to persuade the Europeans to respect the environmental reality, to respect the arguments of Canadians, and to begin to play closer attention to the North Atlantic Fishery Organization quotas that have been set and that they have been ignoring to the detriment of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister said here in the House that the government would act and announce generous wide-ranging programs for the problems we have in the Atlantic fisheries. But what the government announced this morning clearly contradicts the Prime Minister's words. Four hundred and twenty-six million dollars over five years for the Atlantic provinces comes to less than $21 million a year for each province. It is really making fun of us!
Can we then conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister still believes that there is no crisis in the Atlantic fisheries and that everyone seems to be doing fine?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a crisis and there is an answer to this crisis in the Atlantic fishing industry.
Several weeks ago, we announced part of the answer and today some of my colleagues in the Government of Canada announced other measures and programs to

May 7, 1990
Oral Questions
help Canadians in this industry so that they can find other ways to earn their living and also to help establish a strong and lasting industry in the Atlantic region.
Of course, other things must be done. My colleague, the fisheries minister, has called a meeting of the fisheries ministers of the five eastern provinces for Friday. The provinces will also have opportunities to participate in the program to help an industry that is important for all of Canada.
Today we took another very big step to assure Canadians that the industry can continue to play a major role in Canada's future.

Mr. Speaker, they simply want to force us in the Atlantic Provinces to move out.

In the fisheries package announced this morning we see that $130 million is from existing UI and ACOA funds and that $28 million is to replace the tracker surveillance from Summerside.
Can the minister assure us that the remaining $400 million for all the Atlantic provinces over five years is new money and not money being recycled or reprofiled from existing programs? Is that new money?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is a distinction that the hon. member has raised often in the House before and which means nothing at all to the people in Atlantic Canada who, prior to these announcements, were receiving no help and now, because of these announcements, will be receiving in excess of $500 million of help from the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The proposal this morning for Atlantic Canada talks of rebuilding the stocks in order to provide a more reliable economic base for the fishery.
The question is, for whom is this economic base being developed because, as we have already heard, there are people in many small communities who are going to be forced out of the business.
According to the government's own Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council: "The rebuilt
industry-" referring to the fishing industry in the Atlantic, "-should not be dominated by the giants of the industry to the exclusion of the existing participants".
Is this adjustment package not doing just that? In fact, in the long term, is it not simply adjusting the small operators out of the business and saving the field for the larger operators?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer to that question is no. Unfortunately, the leader of the New Democratic Party has her own view as to the point she wants to make and she will not in this case, as in others, be dissuaded by the facts.
The facts are that this is a program designed to re-establish the strength of the Canadian fisheries industry, to re-establish our capacity to enlarge the stocks, or at least to understand more successfully the science relating to a very serious environmental problem that has industrial implications on the east coast of Canada. It is also designed to help individuals who are in the industry and communities that are in the industry, including small communities, look for alternatives that will allow them to maintain, in the fishing industry or in other industries in that region, the kind of viability that they and the people who work in them would like to have.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about economic diversification. However, he will have to acknowledge the fact that the people in the Atlantic region have already said that they want to see a system based on some kind of community allocation of the resource, not just enterprise allocation. Perhaps this government should listen to some of the experts in the field.
I would also like to raise a question with the minister about economic diversification. The same advisory council which I previously mentioned has said to the Minister of Employment, with regard to the regional development programs of this government, that "it appears that certain major negative effects will be experienced as a result of the following federal decisions". They included in that cut-backs to regional development funding and changes to the UI program.
How can the minister claim that economic diversification will work when the very policies of this government have crippled the region?
May 7, 1990

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the very policies of this government have contributed-let me check my figures-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I confess, from time to time, to being overwhelmed by the volume of these figures.
This funding announced today, virtually an additional half a billion dollars going into Atlantic Canada, is in addition to the $2,125 billion the Government of Canada will spend through 1994-1995 on regional development in Atlantic Canada. That is a very significant investment in the economic future of that region. I am sure the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party would acknowledge that point.
It is also an investment designed to try to take account of certain realities that cannot be talked away and that have to be dealt with in Atlantic Canada. These are the realities that have to do with the jobs that are being exercised now by individual Canadians, that have to do with the problems of older Canadians who are in those industries and who need some help in adjustment, and the policies that will be designed to help some of the communities which cannot continue in a fishery where there are fewer and fewer fish and to help some of those industries make use of either other stocks or other attributes of Atlantic Canada.
We believe that there is a very strong and diverse future available to Atlantic Canada. We believe that we have a responsibility to face the facts about the threats and about the responses. That is what we are doing in this program. That is what we have been doing for the other programs this government has followed to help the development of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, earlier the minister spoke about conservation and I want to raise another question about the ability of the government to deal with that particular area and particularly the surveillance of our coast.

This morning, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was talking about the need to guard our coastline. Two years ago, his department admitted that the number of surveillance ships was not sufficient. Dr. Harris said the same in his report. How much money, in dollars and
Oral Questions
cents, is the minister going to spend on marine surveillance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have already mentioned a number of programs to develop our capacity for airborne surveillance. That announcement has already been made. There have been further proposals, by Dr. Harris and others, for dealing with this part of the problem.
However, there is a point I would like to make, since the hon. member mentioned environmental issues. A question was asked earlier today about the reaction of European countries. We are now trying to convince the Europeans that there is a major environmental problem which affects both Europe and Canada. We hope to convince them that they must change the practices of their fisheries and start observing the standards set by the international organization. It is important that Canada speak with one voice on environmental issues concerning the Atlantic.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of a trade delegation from Argentina led by Dr. Eduardo Angeloz, Governor of the Province of Cordoba, and Dr. Adolfo Rodriguez Saa, Governor of the Province of San Luis.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
He will know that for 500 years the fisheries have been the soul and the life-blood of Newfoundland. Yet, in less than a half hour this morning at a news conference in St. John's, his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, effectively placed in jeopardy five centuries of traditional history, an entire way of life.
Has the government actually taken a decision that dozens of our fishing communities must be wiped off the face of the earth? Is that the hidden agenda behind

May 7, 1990
Oral Questions
today's announcement? If so, I say to him, it was not terribly well hidden.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important that the differences between the parties in the House be understood.
The hon. member has said that the fishery in Atlantic Canada is in jeopardy. That is not our view. He has suggested that an industry that has been of crucial importance to Atlantic Canadians since well before they were Canadians is in jeopardy. That is not our view.
We believe that there is an industry that can be made viable in Atlantic Canada. We believe that some realities have to be faced and the government is on the path to facing those realities by working with the people in the fishing industry, by being prepared to put up hundreds of millions of dollars to help, by being prepared to take a look at ways in which we can help older Canadians working in that industry who do not have many other options look at options that they can pursue, and by helping those communities particularly affected by a problem not caused by any government-it is an environmental problem that has reduced fishstocks-and determining ways in which we can help them meet the future effectively.
Rhetoric will not do it. Misreading 500 years of history will not do it. But preparing Atlantic Canada to be able to deal effectively with the next 10 years and the next 100 years is what the government is doing and that is what needs to be done.
Mr. Speaker, that was a marvellous speech. But it was caused by the government allowing the foreign overfishing.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to put his question.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister knows, it will be in jeopardy as long as he continues to use the wrecking ball against the Atlantic fishery.
There are thousands of fixed gear fishermen along the southwest coast who have had serious disastrous catch failures triggering plant shutdowns and thousands of
layoffs. The program today does not mention one solitary word about those people. There is no provision for them at all.
Was that omission an oversight and, if so, will he undertake to have it rectified immediately? Or, was it a deliberate act and part of the government's plans to ensure that these people will be driven out of their communities and put on the welfare rolls in Toronto? If that is what he is up to, he should tell us once and for all.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly tell the House and it is up to the member to decide whether it will be once and for all, or whether we will have to repeat it as we have before.
There is no program by the government to try to depopulate fishing communities in Atlantic Canada. On the contrary, what we are trying to do is to make it possible for those kinds of communities to find an economic future that will last well into the years to come.
The member raises a question as to other issues on the agenda. There certainly are other issues on the agenda, some of which we have to deal with, some of which have to be dealt with by provincial governments, and some by the industry and the people working in it.
My colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, will be convening a meeting of the Atlantic Council of Fisheries Ministers on Friday. There will then be an opportunity, not only to look at other elements of the challenge that remain to be met, but also to begin to discuss how we can fill in the details and the funding of some of the proposals announced this morning and, importantly, Mr. Speaker, how we can ensure that provincial governments, which also have a responsibility for this matter, are able to play their full role.
Why won't you talk to them? You walked away from the table.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This meeting of the council on Friday will continue a pattern of consultation which has been undertaken by my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, on behalf of Canada.
May 7, 1990

My question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. Five weeks have passed since the government announced its program to assist western farmers facing one of the worst financial crises in history, certainly at seeding time, and yet not one dollar of assistance has gone out to farmers.
Western prairie premiers are meeting today in Portage la Prairie and have formed a common front, demanding that the government provide assistance on its own. In view of the common front adopted by the Prairie premiers in demanding that the federal government act on this issue on its own, how and when can farmers expect financial help from the government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite true that the federal government has been there for some five weeks putting its money on the table. We have asked, in the spirit of co-operation and in the spirit of a shared responsibility, that the provinces become a party to the package of assistance that is being worked on.
I can only tell the hon. member that discussions are continuing with the respective agriculture ministers. I have had ongoing discussions with the Ministers of Agriculture for the Provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and, indeed, the Province of Alberta. We are now at the stage where we have looked at the inventory of the provincial programs which are eligible for cost-sharing and progress is being made.
I can also tell him that, in the case of Manitoba, for example, we are at the stage that for an $8 million contribution by the Province of Manitoba, the producers could have something in the area of $72 million distributed almost immediately. So, I ask them to get on board, share their portion of the responsibility, and stop copping-out.

Mr. Speaker, most of the responsibility is with the federal government and the minister knows that.
Oral Questions
Every week, from the farmer's point of view, the news gets worse. The Farm Credit Corporation's interest rate goes up, the initial price of wheat goes down-almost by 20 per cent last week-and still there is no money going to the farmers. Canadian farmers are going to be receiving under initial payment almost one-third less than farmers in the United States.
When is the government going to stop jacking farmers around, stop blaming the provincial premiers, and make the payments to the farmers? Seeding is well under way, initial payments are down, and interest rates are up. When is the government going to make the payments?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not jacking the farmers around. As a matter of fact, we are trying our utmost to ensure that the farmers get as much cash in their hands as soon as they possibly can.
The hon. member knows that the record of the government in terms of support for agriculture has been unprecedented.
Now, Don. When are you going to send out the cheques?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In 1988-1989, for example, in Saskatchewan, the federal government put in $1.7 billion, compared to the Province of Saskatchewan putting in $176 million. That is ten times more than the province put in.
I can refer to Manitoba where in that same year $740 million was provided by the federal government. That is seven times more than that which was provided by the provincial government.
All we are saying, and I ask the hon. member to say with us, it is time that they paid their fair share. That is all we are asking them to do.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is pretty clear to all Canadians that the government is destroying our basic resources, our farms, our fish, and our forests. During National Forestry Week, it is important that we reflect on the importance of those forests.

May 7, 1990
Oral Questions
At the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association's annual meeting on February 2, the Prime Minister said, in reference to forest agreements, that their importance had not diminished around the Cabinet table and that the government was struggling to find funds for them. speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer my colleague from British Columbia. He should be aware that the federal government has done a great deal for forestry. Since 1984, we increased funding by over 300 per cent; we renegotiated the agreements with some provinces, like New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the negotiations are going well now and that the Minister of Forestry is very conscious of the need to give forestry its fair share, since it is one of the most important sectors of the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
In his question, my colleague from Prince George- Bulkley Valley referred to unrenewed forest agreements. As the minister knows, in western Canada these agreements are only part of 26 agreements worth $671 million that have expired since March 31,1989, and have not been renewed. speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to initiate the response from the government to the second message from the other place respecting Bill C-21, An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.
I must begin by noting that once again,-a bill to provide new unemployment insurance benefits and to provide additional resources for training-a bill which meets the real needs of Canadian workers-has been needlessly delayed.

The benefits and the imperative to meet the needs of workers in Canada have been lost in the storm of rhetoric which has surrounded this bill. Many of our critics seem to believe that nothing in the world has changed, and that our training and unemployment insurance policies need not change either. Perhaps worse still is that the critics, both in this House and outside, are prepared to accept the argument of the unelected Liberal senators that the Senate has used, and ought to use, a power to change the spending priorities of an elected government.
Even those who, as a matter of principle, have traditionally opposed the exercise of power by an unelected Senate, have now given precedence to expediency because it suits their immediate purposes. We believe that the use of that power by the Senate is unconscionable on moral and democratic grounds, and that it is unacceptable on policy grounds.
If we in this Chamber, not just the government, but all of us, accept the message from the Senate, the situation of working Canadian women and men will deteriorate, and the powers of the House of Commons will be eroded for partisan, political and manipulative purposes. This Chamber, and all of us in it representing our constituents, have the opportunity to rise above such narrow and misguided thinking. It has the chance to help Canadian workers and their employers face the challenges of a world market-place as we head toward another century.
It is my intention today to draw the attention of members to the issues, and what is really at the heart of this government's bill. Members of this House must understand that continued inaction poses a very real
Government Orders
threat to Canadian workers from coast to coast. Members of this House must continue to oppose the shortsighted and opportunistic stance taken by the opponents of this bill.

After outlining the benefits that will come from Bill C-21,1 will then respond, in detail, to the message from the Senate.
First, however, I feel compelled to comment on the constitutional situation which faces all of us.
Let me remind hon. members that the Hon. Speaker advised that only we in this House can break the impasse over this issue.
This House, and this House alone, can define its rights and privileges and this House and this House alone can defend itself against the actions of those unelected persons in the other place.
This House must defend its historic right to initiate and direct the financial policy of the elected government. This is not simply a theoretical exercise, but a defence of one of the key principles of responsible government. The battle for this right was won generations ago and we must protect its integrity.
The budgetary power is not one that governments take lightly. It is one for which we are accountable to the Canadian people, as is every government which receives its authority from the ballot box.

Those in the other place do not have the same form of accountability and this House cannot let them take that authority from us. This government is simply not prepared to abandon its responsibilities by acceding to the demands of a group of Liberal senators who are caught in some historical time warp. This is not a time for anachronism, it is a time for action.

Let me remind members of the point raised in the ruling of the Hon. Speaker last Thursday, when he cited experts in the field.
The Senate has- accepted as binding on itself the proposition that it should not unduly disturb what has come to be called "the balance of ways and means" or, as Hopkins says, "that it would be inadmissible to tamper with the overall financial program submitted by the government in its budgetary proposals in such a way as to effect a material change in the budgetary surplus or deficit".

May 7, 1990

Yet, that is precisely what they wish to do with this bill.
Liberal senators claim that they have public support for their actions and their threats. We understand better than most that some people and groups do not support some elements in this bill. Thoughtful analysts all recognize that there is a very real difference between expressing concern about this legislation and supporting unelected Senators as they attack the rights of the elected Chamber. That understanding has been echoed in editorials and columns in newspapers all across this country as recently as this weekend. We have something from The Ottawa Citizen, The Toronto Star, The Gazette in Montreal. We have another column in The Toronto Star and we have something from The Financial Post. This is just in the last few days, Mr. Speaker. We have all these over the last few months.
That is the kind of thoughtful analysis around this kind of issue that is important to all of us on all sides of the House, and they have all called on the Senate to recognize that it is not playing its legitimate role in what it is doing in this debate. There is a large body of well-informed opinion that understands, even if some Liberals in the Senate do not, that what that Chamber claims it can do has no relationship to what it should do.
Perhaps most important, and perhaps what it should not do the most, is to presume to tell this House how many dollars to spend. Dollars, let me remind everyone, that come from the taxpayers who elected us in this Chamber. This House adopted the budget of April 27, 1989, and Bill C-21 is an integral part of that decision. With this message the Liberals in the Senate want us to increase those expenditures under that budget by about $1.75 billion a year.
On what basis, what authority? My colleagues say we cannot afford it. Also, on what basis and what authority can they make this claim? I ask that particularly of the members of the NDP to answer today. As the hon. speaker noted in Britain in the Mother of Parliaments, the Upper House ceded its right to reject or amend money bills like C-21 in 1911. Mr. Speaker, that is even before you and I were born.
Unfortunately we have yet to see such a concession to responsible and representative government in this country-at least officially. However, if one reviews the record of the other place and the decisions during periods of Liberal governments in the past half century, one finds a striking respect for the British tradition.

Our government has a mandate to act and Bill C-21 flows directly from that mandate. This bill is part of our commitment specifically to provide Canadians with the best training and adjustment programs possible and more generally with our policies for economic renewal.
Canadians understand that. While Liberal Senators appeal to special interest groups to make hollow claims about the support of Canadians for their anti-democratic actions, we know differently.

Recent public opinion polls have shown that a strong majority of Canadians support the idea of using UI funds to train unemployed people so that they can find and keep better jobs. Last year, for example, a Decima poll and a study by Environics each found that about two-thirds of Canadians supported our plans to shift UI funds to job training programs. A more recent Decima poll confirmed that degree of support.

Canadians want to know that the UI system is being used properly and effectively. Bill C-21 offers proper and effective uses and it builds on our experience with employment programs.
When this government took office in 1984, we looked at the range of programs and services in place to train workers and to support the economic development of communities across this country.
We saw that the old style of job creation and training programs simply did not reflect the needs of a changing economy. Obviously, programs which did not reflect genuine economic needs could not meet the needs of workers who looked to the government for assistance.
Our government recognized this problem and it acted. The result was the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which has been a successful response to the requirement for a modern workforce.
May 7, 1990

CJS has broken the "makework" stigma of previous programs. It has resulted in success stories all across this country-because those programs reflected real requirements for training and upgrading workers.
CJS marked the creation of a partnership between the private and public sectors to meet labour market challenges.
Still, with experience, it became clear that more could be done and more had to be done.

Something that we concern ourselves about is that worker productivity is one of the basic criteria for competitiveness in the world economy today. I think we would all agree on that in this Chamber. For that reason, it should concern all members of this House that the productivity of Canadian workers has grown much more slowly than that of workers in Japan, Germany and the United Kingdom.
When we recognize that investment in training is a key to increased productivity, we must ask how Canada fares. The sorry fact is that Canadian employers lag behind those in other countries when it comes to training their employees. We have had discussions on what comes from Statistics Canada as to which peoples and numbers are more accurate, the private sector's or ours, but however it is measured, the important point is that Canada is low. That is simply in today's world unacceptable.
The Canadian labour markets needs an active labour market policy, not a passive one, that assists the private sector, workers and employers, to respond to the increasing pace of change in the labour force created by the global economy. An active labour market policy draws on all tools to help workers and employers to adapt to changing situations.

On April 11, 1989, I announced plans for just such a policy, the Labour Force Development Strategy. Bill C-21 will give that policy life.
I would like to bring members up-to-date on some of the steps which have been taken so far with the LFDS, and to underline the important work which remains to be done, work which cannot take place until C-21 has been passed.

The Labour Force Development Strategy is made up of a variety of components which build on our experience with training Canadian workers.
The success of CJS partnerships provided a foundation for more significant changes in labour market policy. These changes will assist the Canadian private sector in developing a training culture-an approach which places a real value on improving the skills which workers bring to their jobs.
Members should recognize that this partnership is at the core of LFDS, but until C-21 has been passed by both Houses, we can only take tentative steps.
Some have already been taken. To ensure the success of LFDS, I wanted advice not only from officials but from the people who depend most on the success of our employment policies. I wanted to hear what business and labour had to say, in concrete terms, about labour market needs.
To that end, we sponsored a series of task forces under the auspices of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre. They have recently completed reviews of many areas of labour market policies, programs and services. They have provided me with valuable advice. But until this bill passes, it can only stay advice. In fact, if the Liberals in the Senate carry out their threats to defeat this bill, then the entire exercise will have been a waste, not just of time and energy, but a waste of the futures of many working Canadians.

Here is the report to which I am referring, full of good recommendations for Canadian workers. We urgently need to implement new programs for Canadian workers. We also need to expand existing programs which have proven their value.
First, we must do more in Canada in the area of human resource planning. Employers used to be able to count on an increasing stream of young workers who could learn simple jobs quickly and who, year after year, came out of school into the labour force. Those days are over. Occupations now require more skills and more training and at the same time the number of young people entering the work force is declining. Employers no longer have the luxury of that broad choice of young people.

May 7, 1990
Government Orders
Effective human resource planning is a partial answer to those programs. Employers and workers need to know what skills are going to be required and how to prepare themselves accordingly. Our labour force development strategy will provide funding to encourage such planning.
We have already had success with groups in industries such as automotive repair and services, electrical and electronic manufacturing, in helping them to identify the skills that are needed in years to come and to take action to meet those needs. Passage of Bill C-21 will allow us to expand those efforts greatly.
Human resource planning also allows us to address another important issue, something I would think that the NDP also would be particularly interested in, and that is employment equity. Aboriginals, women, disabled Canadians, new Canadians and older workers have been shut out of many skilled jobs. That is wrong from the standpoint of fairness and it is also wrong for Canada economically. Human resource planning, making business and the workplace part of the solution can address this problem and it will ensure that all Canadians have a chance for the good jobs of tomorrow. However, the financial resources which we need to carry out this work are inadequate for the task as long as C-21 remains in limbo.
Another aspect of labour force development would be improvements to entry level training. Increased qualifications for jobs have meant that too many of our young people lack the skills to meet even the most basic requirements of employers today.
Some months ago I announced the Stay-in-School program that will encourage young people to finish their high school education. The LFDS will ensure that students have the basic skills needed to help enter a more complicated job market. For instance, LFDS will allow the government to quadruple its support for co-op education. That has proven to be a valuable program for youth.
We will work with the provinces and territories to improve programs like apprenticeship. Again, those programs need funds and, again, we need Bill C-21 to provide those funds.

Third, many members will be aware of the work of Employment and Immigration's Industrial Adjustment
Service. Staff from IAS work with employers and workers facing major changes such as large-scale expansions or layoffs.
Through LFDS, we have proposed to double the funds available to this service.

The fourth item, one that is of particular interest to members on all sides of the House in all regions of Canada, is Community Futures. It is one of our most productive tools to assist small and rural communities. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is one of the most productive tools of any government in the history of Canada. Experience proves that the best economic plans are those that are developed by the people in a community, wherever it may be, and members on all sides of the House have strongly supported and lauded the Community Futures Program. Bill C-21 would provide an additional $50 million for this program for over 200 communities.
I see people in the Chamber today who are looking for assistance for their communities, who have benefited from this program in the past, and, under Bill C-21, who will benefit from it in the future.
In addition to improvements in existing programs, we propose to do much more through the Labour Force Development Strategy to help those who are unemployed. The Unemployment Insurance Program has been in place in Canada for 50 years. But it is no longer enough today just to provide cash to the unemployed. We have to do more. We have to offer these people a way out of unemployment. We have to offer them a better future, more secure and more stable.
So what are we going to do? First, an additional 60,000 people could receive training, in addition to their UI benefits, if Bill C-21 passes. We intend to devote $350 million-are you listening over there?-

-to this training effort. That is $350 million to meet a demand that is evident across the country. Unemployed people have told us through our labour market surveys that they know themselves that they cannot get jobs because they do not have the skills and that they want those skills.
Second, many more Canadians would be able to start their own businesses through the use of UI funds, or to move to areas where jobs are more plentiful. That does
May 7, 1990

not necessarily mean across the country, but maybe within their own region or province. We have proposed to set aside $45 million for those programs. We cannot act until this bill passes.
On another front, one of the most exciting developments that the government has introduced in job training has been the joint federal-provincial efforts to help social assistance recipients escape from the welfare trap. In towns and cities all across Canada, thousands of men and women have received the help they asked for to learn the skills necessary to improve their lives and the lives of their families in the future by getting themselves out of that welfare system.
The LFDS would allocate an additional $50 million to this program for some of the poorest people in our country. With matching contributions from the Canada Assistance Plan, from the provinces and territories, a total of 200 million new dollars could be right there, ready to go into action on behalf of these people. That money could be at work now if we had moved on this bill. It is not at work now and every day of delay impedes the abilities of Canadians in the most difficult circumstances, to build better lives for themselves and their loved ones.

Older workers represent a special case. Most members have been approached by constituents who have lost jobs that they had held for many years. Older workers can face a difficult time finding new jobs for many reasons.
LFDS contains measures which would help these people in addition to the other retraining programs. One hundred million dollars would be available-$100 million-if C-21 were implemented. We could be implementing these programs today. We are not. And every day that we are held back, is another day in which unemployed people are left to live with a situation we all know is unsatisfactory.

Members will be well aware that much of our training activity is done in co-operation with other levels of government. Community colleges and training councils across the country have the expertise so necessary for these programs. In the past, we have developed individu-

al agreements with provinces and territories which respect the interests and the contributions of both parties.
In January, we embarked on negotiations for a new generation of training agreements that will represent what the provinces themselves have accurately described as a new partnership. There is general agreement that the prospects for this partnership are excellent.
Elowever, in the absence of Bill C-21, the resources that we bring to this task will be severely limited. That is why the provinces are anxiously awaiting this bill, so that we can get on with that job.
Since our debate today is a result of the action of Liberal senators, it is worth taking a moment to review what we have agreed to previously. I understand the role of the other place, as we all do. When the Senate sent its first message to the House, the government found some issues to which it was prepared to agree. We agreed to affirm explicitly that basic skills and literacy training could be funded. We felt that that was implicit but agreed to put that in for greater clarity.
We agreed to provide greater detail in the annual developmental uses plan which would show how the government intended to use the money provided under the UI Act, and we agreed that any proposed repeal of the system of UI benefits for self-employed fishermen would require parliamentary approval. We agreed.
Despite our sincere attempts to accommodate the concerns expressed, the Liberals in the Senate have simply chosen, virtually to reiterate all of their original demands.

Recommendations 2(a), (b) and (c) in the message would eliminate the government's ability to pay for some types of help to workers from the UI account.
In the bill, this House agreed that it was reasonable to call on the UI fund for certain types of payments-ones which were an investment in people's futures.
We agreed that the cost of training course, the cost of relocating people to areas where their chances of finding work are better, allowing workers to use UI benefits to fund self-employment or for earnings supplements were all appropriate measures.

May 7, 1990
Government Orders
The Liberals in the Senate disagree. They prefer to see the deficit rise to pay for these improvements.

As a responsible government, we cannot allow that to happen. We believe it is better to use UI funds for this sort of active assistance to help people stay off UI permanently.
It is not only this government that believes in innovative uses. Let me quote the Premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Wells. When we proposed this change, Mr. Wells said: "I must say that I think it indicates that the federal government is going in the right direction-and that is just what I have been asking for."
Members in the House should reflect on Mr. Wells' other comments in which he saw this use of UI as a springboard for economic development. He said: "That is the kind of thing we will be using, what will otherwise be paid out as unemployment insurance to provide meaningful long-term employment."
I do not very often agree with Premier Wells, but I agree with him on this. I would think that people of the same political persuasion might take a look at this. I hope that Premier Wells' province and others will find ways to work with people who want to take advantage of the opportunities that Bill C-21 will provide. But first, we need this bill to become law.
We continue to oppose Recommendations 3(a) and (b). The latter is a minor wording change related to Recommendation 2. The other recommendation, 3(a), seeks to impose a new level of bureaucracy on the process of helping people to take advantage of the new opportunities that Bill C-21 will offer. By creating a complex appeal system on an issue that really does not lend itself to adjudication, precious time and money will be lost.
This recommendation also would prevent the government from designing the special programs needed to help the unemployed which is what this bill is all about. Let me give you an example.
A skilled worker is laid off from the factory where he or she has worked for many years. That worker has never been unemployed before and wants to go back to work. He or she has thought about the possibility of starting a business. The way the law is written right now, if the worker does that, he or she will be cut off from unemployment insurance because the act says that people have to be available for work. Clearly, self-employed people are not available to seek work from other people.
I do not think that my hypothetical worker should have to go through that. I think my worker should have that choice. The government thinks that that is only fair, and we want to have the ability to write special rules for cases like this. If the House accepts Recommendation 3(a), there will be no special rules to help these workers. Bill C-21 will give us that ability.
Recommendations 4 (c) and 4 (d) deal with issues on which we have made some concessions to the Senate during our last debate on this subject. We have agreed to provide greater detail in the annual developmental uses plan.

However, we cannot accept the degree of detail that the Liberal Senators have demanded. We cannot take a plan that is intended to be responsive and flexible to changing economic needs and force it into a kind of straitjacket that has been fastened by the people in the other place.
Let me explain that a developmental plan is just that. It is a plan that would be developed months before the fiscal year begins and while one could project probable expenditures by a province, it would be nearly impossible to try and estimate how much would be spent in each town or each economic region.
What the Liberals in the Senate want us to say is: "We're sorry, we would really like to help you, but when we developed our plan last year we did not really know that your main employer was going to require skill training to double his work force or was going to move his plant". That would be the impact of that recommendation.
Under our proposal we would have the ability to move funds to the areas where the needs are the greatest during the fiscal year. That is simply good management.
To do what the Liberals want is to force people and communities to fit our programs. We want programs to fit people. Further, we could never give those same Senators the veto over the developmental uses plan that they demand. They point out that there are precedents for Senate veto and they promised to use it judicially. I
May 7, 1990

think that members in this House can only reflect on our current debate to question that promise.
With recommendations 5(a) and 5(b) we come to the question of people who quit their jobs without cause and who expect the UI system to support them. More than $1 billion goes to these people annually. Right now they face a disqualification period of between one and six weeks. We are proposing to increase that to seven to 12 weeks and to restrict the amount of benefits they would get when they do become eligible.
We recognize that certain conditions can force people to quit jobs and that is why in the original bill we talked about "without just cause" because the assumption was that there is of course just cause. However, at report stage I accepted the comments made by many witnesses before the legislative committee regarding the need to identify and strengthen what those causes may be and those who quit for reasons such as, for example, sexual harassment, something to which we are very sensitive.
Once again, that had been our intent and we did it for greater clarity. It will protect claimants who had no reasonable choice but to quit. They will not have to serve a disqualification period.
Claimants who do quit jobs without just cause may find another one before the disqualification has been completely served. In those cases, we have proposed to carry over the unserved part of the disqualification to the next claim that the person makes. If the claimant works for 20 weeks we waive the penalty. But if not, we would propose to carry it over for up to six years.
The Senate had asked us in recommendation 5(b) to reduce this to two years and we agreed to this recommendation. We did not agree to it in the previous message because it will have some impact on our ability to fund the Labour Force Development Strategy. I would remind members that every dollar we take off the one side is not available for the other side. But we do recognize the value of compromise and we are committed to some very fundamental principles, but we are not intransigent. For that reason we are going to accept this recommendation.
However, I would like to underscore for this Chamber that in virtually every other country people who quit their job voluntarily never have access to unemployment

insurance. We are one of the very few countries that does that at all, for cause or not for cause.
Recommendation six would inhibit our ability to form effective partnerships with other groups interested in training.
In the Labour Force Development Strategy we envision contracts with outside groups to provide training or other services. These are legitimate costs to program administration, as if they were being carried out in Canada Employment Centres. And we believe they should be treated in a similar manner to other administrative costs. Liberal senators think not. They would rather cut the money available for developmental uses by forcing these costs into that budget.
Every dollar for administration is a dollar not spent on training. For that reason, members will understand why this recommendation cannot be accepted by this House.
Recommendation seven is one which attempts to overturn the right of the elected House to set a budget and to act on it.
In recognition of current fiscal realities, we have decided that the federal government cannot continue to contribute to the UI account. We have determined that the people who benefit, whether they are workers who can count on support from UI when they become unemployed-remember it is employed people who pay the premiums-or employers who know that UI can help them keep good workers, can and must pay for the system which provides those benefits.
The Liberals in the other place have said that they do not agree. They believe that spending an additional $1.75 billion a year from general revenues makes sense. They believe that pushing up the deficit to pay for these benefits also makes sense.
It is exactly that kind of financial thinking that got this country into the mess we are trying to clean up. We cannot accept that kind of short-sighted thinking. I would remind them as well that in a way we are talking about the same pocket. Who pays taxes? Businesses and people who are working pay taxes. Who pays premiums for unemployment insurance? Businesses, employers who pay the higher proportion and workers who are employed. We are talking about the same pocket. We are talking about the same people. That is something that this government understands. There is only one taxpayer

out there and he or she pays either way. By doing it this way we do not add to the deficit.
This government was elected in 1984 and again in 1988 largely because Canadians understood which party could be counted on to manage effectively.
I do not have to dwell on the strides this government has made in controlling the growth of public expenditures to bring the deficit in line. However, I should point out to hon. members opposite that they should tell their colleagues in the other place that recommendations like these can only weaken Canada's economy by driving up government spending, or driving up the deficit.
We cannot accept the demand that we spend more, nor can we accept what is a veiled claim to power. As you yourself, Mr. Speaker, stated in your eloquent ruling:
There are many Canadians-who have no idea whatsoever of the
awesome powers which the Senate claims to itself over the elected
lower House.
You also noted that the House for many years had defended its rightful role against these claims. Sir Wilfrid Laurier did just that in 1917 and we must do the same today. Some Liberal senators have said the same thing. I quote Senator MacEachen speaking on a borrowing bill in 1985: "I think if we did amend the bill in any serious way, or if we defeated it, I think that would be quite arrogant". Let me quote Senator Frith: "There may be 100 reasons why we should not in the Senate yield to the House and only one reason why we should, and if that one reason is that the Commons is elected and the Senate is not, then that is reason enough to yield". That is what we are talking about here today.
Let me go on to Recommendation eight, which deals with benefits for fishermen. Because of our continued concern about the viability of the fishing industry, our government has taken action on a number of fronts, as we have seen even today. Yet we still see Liberal Senators and other groups spread fear among people for blatantly partisan ends.
Let me state again what I have stated before. Fishermen will not see their benefits disappear. In the interests of conciliation however-and I am a conciliatory person,
Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you and many others would acknowledge- we have decided to respond to the Senate's continued concerns about the regulations which govern benefits for self-employed fishermen.
The government is determined to respond constructively to the needs of fishermen, and I say that in all seriousness. We recognize that UI plays an important role in the economies of their communities.
For these reasons, we will amend the bill to ensure that the House of Commons has a full opportunity to review and debate any changes to regulations on fishermen's benefits.
For reasons noted earlier, I cannot, in all good conscience, extend the power to review these regulations to the Senate.
Elected members, and remember that is what we have been talking about today, who are directly accountable for their actions to the people of Canada, are the people who should take those important decisions.
Those who owe their office to appointment, capable as they may be, and I would certainly recognize that there are many capable people in the other place, do not have the same accountability and they cannot be given the same powers.
With Recommendation nine, we return to the fiscal issue that I raised while discussing Recommendation seven. Whether Liberal Senators choose to accept it or not, the fact of the matter is that this government has had to make hard decisions regarding where best to use very limited funds.
Previous Liberal governments, including the one in which Senator MacEachen was Minister of Finance, shrank from those decisions when they had an opportunity to act responsibly.
What was the result? It was a veritable mountain of debt. Yet they lecture this House on fiscal responsibility. We do not find that acceptable. Also, we believe that the cost to UI premium payers for fishing benefits are so small, amounting to a little over 2 cents of every UI dollar, so let us keep this in perspective. Those benefits do not place an unreasonable burden on the UI account.
May 7, 1990

In summary, for all of the reasons I outlined, we cannot accept the bulk of the message which was sent to us by the other place, although we are sending back some agreement with some of the things that they have suggested in a conciliatory mode.
Too many of the recommendations are based on the notion that the unelected Chamber can order the elected Chamber to make expenditures that the country cannot afford. We have rejected that view consistently in the past and we must reject it now.
Too many other recommendations seek to give the Senate powers it does not warrant in a democratic system of government. Having reviewed the contents of the message from the Senate and remembering the many valuable and necessary initiatives that are contained in the Labour Force Development Strategy, what course of action should the House follow?
Virtually everyone who has commented on this bill has supported the need for more training and more support for a training culture in Canadian business among Canadian workers.
They have been less forthcoming on how these initiatives should be financed. Even this report, which comes up with many recommendations that we are finding very useful, does not come up with an alternative way of financing the system that is going to be acceptable to Canadians. Virtually everyone who has commented on this bill is in the same position.
We believe that modifications to the UI system are an appropriate vehicle for this process. As I pointed out, both workers and employers will benefit from the LFDS, and through unemployment insurance we are asking them to pay for the benefits to which they are entitled. We think those should be good benefits.
As well, we have proposed some changes to the existing range of UI benefits. These will require claimants to work somewhat longer in many areas of the country to be eligible. The duration of benefits will be reduced slightly. Penalties for people who quit their jobs without good reason will be increased.
We have designed these changes with great sensitivity to regional differences. The greatest impact will be in places like Toronto and southern Ontario where unemployment remains low. We have been very careful to
Government Orders
minimize the effects of these changes in regions where seasonal employment and historic structural problems have resulted in higher levels of unemployment. On the benefit side, that is where many of the benefits will fall.
Despite the exaggerated claims made by many critics of this bill, I firmly believe that the impact of these changes will be very modest. Certainly, compared with changes made in the late 1970s, they are not onerous. However they will be sufficient to generate the funds necessary for the progress that the LFDS will generate.
It is not sufficient merely to favour training. One must have a clear sense of how to pay for it in a way that is not administratively difficult or too costly. While there have been many suggestions, there has been no consensus on an alternative to the one we have proposed.
There is no time to waste in implementing the LFDS. Each day we continue with this discussion is a day in which our competitors on this continent, in Europe, and in Asia surpass us in their abilities to compete.
The real needs of Canadian working men and women will not be addressed by pretending that nothing has changed and that the same old policies must be maintained, that they are written on some kind of stone tablet. The real needs of the Canadian labour force will not be addressed by pretending that the public sector and the private sector have different agendas.

Mr. Speaker, this government introduced Bill C-21 to allow it to make some modest, but needed, changes in its unemployment insurance program and to initiate some major improvements in the development of Canada's labour force. C-21 recognizes that in a world of change, success will go to those countries which adapt best.
[English)
The government is determined that Canada will succeed in that new world. This government is equally determined that the Senate is not going to stand in the way of that success. And this government is determined to protect the rights and privileges of members of this Chamber not just on this side of the House but on that side of the House, all the way down both sides. To make the policy and program decisions that this country needs is what we intend to do.
