(4)	A regulation referred to in subsection (3) shall come into force on the tenth sitting day after the day on which it is tabled, or on any later day that is specified in the regulation, unless a motion to revoke it, signed by not fewer than thirty members of the House of Commons, is filed with the Speaker of the House of Commons before the tenth sitting day.
(5)	Where a motion to revoke a regulation is filed with the Speaker of the House of Commons pursuant to subsection (4), it shall be taken up and considered by the House of Commons within five sitting days after the day on which it is filed.

(6)	A motion taken up and considered in accordance with subsection (5) shall be taken up after the ordinary hour of daily adjournment, for a period not exceeding four hours and at the end of the debate the Speaker of the House of Commons shall, forthwith, without further debate or amendment, put every question necessary for the disposition of the motion.
(7)	Where a motion to revoke a regulation is adopted, the regulation is revoked and where the motion is defeated, the regulation shall come into force on the day after the day on which the motion is defeated or on any later day that is specified in the regulation.
(8)	Where Parliament is prorogued or dissolved before a motion to revoke a regulation is disposed of or, if no such motion has been filed, before the end of the period referred to in subsection (4), the regulation is deemed to be revoked.
(9)	For the purpose of this section, 'sitting day' means a day on which the House of Commons is sitting."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are debating Bill C-21, this Conservative government's bill to cut back massively on our unemployment insurance program by $1.3 billion at a time when we still have over one million unemployed in this country and at a time when the Minister of Finance in his recent budget has predicted an unemployment rate of 8.5 per cent in this year.
The government is proposing these cuts at this particular time when we have such a large number of unemployed. The government intends to implement these cuts of $1.3 billion in our unemployment insurance program by first of all making it more difficult for Canadians to qualify for unemployment insurance by requiring a
May 7, 1990

longer period of work in order to be eligible for unemployment insurance. By doing that, of course fewer will qualify and the government will save money.
Second, in this bill the government is shortening the benefit period which will be available to unemployed Canadians under the unemployment insurance program. By doing that the government will save money once again.
Third, the government is withdrawing its contribution to the unemployment insurance fund which last year was $2.5 billion. I should point out that since the very beginning of unemployment insurance the unemployment insurance fund has been financed from three sources. It has been financed by workers who, when they are employed, pay a certain percentage each month to the unemployment insurance fund. It is financed, as well, by employers who pay a certain percentage each month to the fund, but it has also been financed by the government.
As I pointed out, in the last fiscal year the contribution was $2.5 billion, and in this bill the government is terminating that contribution to the fund. This means that from now on, if this bill passes, the fund must be totally supported by workers and employers.
Fourth, the government is cutting back on the program by increasing the penalties for people who voluntarily quit their employment, without, in my opinion and in the opinion of many Canadians, adequately considering the reasons for those voluntary quits.
As the minister points out, the government has bent a bit, has made a few amendments to recognize voluntary quits for sexual harassment and so on, but they do not go far enough and the penalty that the government has in place in still too high. As a result of this bill 155,000 Canadians will totally lose their unemployment insurance benefits, that is 155,000 who would have qualified under the present law will lose under this law, and 775,000 will partially lose their benefits.
The impact on our provinces will be severe. For example, according to the impact study of the Canadian Labour Congress-and the government has not presented an impact study to challenge the Canadian Labour Congress study-as a result of this bill Newfoundland will lose $51 million. In other words, $51 million a year
Government Orders
that would go into that province will not now go in because of this bill. Prince Edward Island will lose $32 million. Nova Scotia will lose $29 million. New Brunswick will lose $148 million; Quebec, $224 million, and it goes on.
As you can see, those provinces with the highest rates of unemployment will be hit very hard and will lose a lot of money that otherwise would have helped maintain industry, individuals and families in those provinces.
What will be the result of these cutbacks? Through this bill the government is going to make it more difficult to qualify for unemployment insurance. The government is going to shorten the benefit period.
This will mean that there will be people without work who will not have the benefit of unemployment insurance. What will happen to them? Are we going to allow these people to starve? Are we going to force them to soup kitchens? Are we going to force them on bread lines? No, that is not our way.
As a result of this bill and these cutbacks, these people who are unemployed but who will not have unemployment insurance will be forced onto the welfare rolls. Who pays for welfare? In most provinces it is the provincial government. In some provinces, like Ontario and Nova Scotia, I believe, it is the provinces and the municipalities. Somebody will have to take care of these unemployed people but the federal government is shifting the burden from the unemployment insurance system to the welfare system where there are means tests, where the amount of support is lower, and where the province has to pick up the tab.
It is true that provincial welfare systems are financed to approximately 50 per cent by the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan, but still, that is a cutback by the federal government with respect to assistance for the unemployed.
Many municipalities that appeared before the parliamentary committee pointed out that their welfare bills, as well as the welfare bills of the provinces, will increase considerably if this bill passes because there will be a larger number of unemployed Canadians who will have to live without the help of unemployment insurance.

The minister admits, although she tries to hide it in her rhetoric-and I just listened to her speech-that the government is cutting $1.3 billion from the unemployment insurance fund. She tries to justify this bill by saying that $800 million of those moneys will be redirected to training.
The minister goes on at great length to argue how important training is. She is wasting her breath on us. We agree that training is important. Training is extremely important. We believe in putting large sums of money into training, but we believe in putting it into training as it was always done in this country, and that is out of general tax revenues, not out of the unemployment insurance fund.
The minister and the government members attempt to pretend that we must make a choice in this country between unemployment insurance and training. In other words, if you want to have training, you must cut back on unemployment insurance. If you want higher unemployment insurance, you will have less training. I just heard her a few minutes ago saying that if this bill is not passed, there will not be this kind of training or that kind of training.
That is a false dilemma. That is not the choice that should be put to Canadians. We have always had in this country a strong program of training, but we have also continued to improve our unemployment insurance program.
The government's commitment to training now, with this Bill C-21, is a phoney commitment, and I will demonstrate that. In 1984, when the Conservatives took over the government of this country, the federal training bill was $2.2 billion. Between 1984 and 1989 the government cut that training program by 32 per cent from $2.2 billion to $1.5 billion. It cut training programs by $700 million. This is a government that today would have us believe that training is a most wonderful thing and that it has always been committed to it. That is a phoney position of the government. The only reason it is now trying to put money into training is that it set up this de Grandpre commission to investigate how the government and the country was to deal with the threat of U.S.-Canada free trade on our Canadian workers. In that report Mr. de Grandpre and his commissioners, in several recommendations, said that more money had to
be put into training, otherwise jobs would leave Canada and go to the United States, that industries would shift from Canada to the United States.
So all of a sudden the government said: "Gosh, we have done the wrong thing for the last five years. We have been cutting training by 32 per cent, from $2.2 billion to $1.7 billion, by $700 million, and now we have to find money to put more money back into training". The highest priority of this government is not people, but the deficit. It said: "What will we do?" It looked around and found that the only place it could find the money for that was to take it out of the unemployment insurance fund. In other words, the government decided that in order to pay for training it had to reduce the money available to unemployed Canadians, money they need when they are out of work to pay for their groceries, their rent and to send their children school and so on. The government took that money, from a source that was never touched, to use as a principal means of paying for training. That is why we are opposed to the bill and why many Canadians are opposed to the bill.
When the minister stands up in this House and argues passionately for training, that is a phoney and false argument. None of us are opposed to training. What we are opposed to is taking money out of a fund that is supposed to support people when they are unemployed.
I mentioned previously that the government is also cutting its contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. I said that last year that contribution was $2.5 billion. The minister and other members of the government have alleged that the principal purpose of this bill is to shift money into training, by taking those moneys that were paid in premiums by workers and employers and putting them into a fund for training. Why should training only be paid for by workers and employers? On what principle should only workers and employers pay for training that is very much required if we are to have a modern, progressive economy?
We have never said that education should only be paid for by parents and by students. If we were to say that, that would be using a similar argument to that which the government is using. We say that education should be paid for by all taxpayers because education benefits everybody. Education not only benefits the student who studies and the parents who have children in school, it
May 7, 1990

benefits everybody including parents who have no children, and corporations. By that same principle, training should be paid for by everybody out of general tax revenue and not out of a fund that was contributed to by workers and employers for unemployment insurance benefits.
The unemployment insurance program was established in 1940 following the Great Depression of the 1930s. It was established because it was found to be essential that when the economy went into a slow period there be a means of keeping workers and their families financially soluble so that they could pay for the essentials of life. As I said previously, the purpose of the fund was to make sure that unemployed workers would be able to pay for their food, rent, clothing, transportation to work, their children's schooling and the other essentials of life.
That is what the program has been since the 1940s. In the Great Depression of the 1930s, when we did not have unemployment insurance, workers who were unemployed had to rely on bread lines, soup kitchens and charity. It was thought that never again should we have to rely on that system but that we should have a progressive, substantial and sound unemployment insurance system. Since 1940 we have been improving the system, except now we have a government that is cutting it back.
The government says that this bill is essential because we must develop a better system of training, that we must put more money into training. None of the groups in the country that oppose this bill would oppose more money for training. They all say, as we say, that the money for training should come out of general revenue.
Let me put forward another argument which demonstrates how bad this bill is and why it is wrong to take the money away from unemployed workers to pay for training. In the hearings that we had before the House of Commons parliamentary committee on this bill it was pointed out to us time and again that many of the workers who are unemployed are already trained. They are skilled machinists, skilled electricians, accountants. In other words, they have many skills. The reason for their unemployment is not that they do not have skill,
Government Orders
the reasons for their unemployment is that there are no jobs in the place where they live.

speechtext: I said you are silly.

speechtext:
That is typical of the attitude of Tories in this country. They would have us believe that all the unemployed in this country have no skills and are not trained and that the solution to their unemployment is simply to give them training and they will have a job. That is total nonsense and anybody who knows this country knows that to be true.
We visited every province of this country and example after example was given to us of the fact that Canada has many resource-based towns. We have many towns and cities that rely on the mining industry, the forest industry, on fishing and farming. When that particular industry goes down, the whole community goes down, and the people who go down in that community for the most part are not untrained. Many of them have very high skills.
The government is suggesting that if we trained all the people in a mining town where there is unemployment, those people will find jobs. That is nonsense, unless they all move away from that community and go to Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary, and even then it is questionable whether they will find jobs. The fact of the matter is that the solution to unemployment in many cases is not more training. Even where the solution is more training, it also requires jobs.
Let us take the example of Canso, Nova Scotia, or Summerside, Prince Edward Island. If we simply retrained the people in those communities and paid no attention to putting jobs into those communities, what good would this new training be to those workers? I suppose the suggestion of Tories would be, again, to move to upper Canada or move away from your own town, your own city, your own province. That is wrong and Canadian after Canadian said it is wrong. That is the message they have been trying to give this government. They are saying that training is a good thing but we should not take the money for training out of the unemployment insurance fund and, in addition, training is not the solution to unemployment. The solution to unemployment is jobs because many of the people who

May 7, 1990
Government Orders
are unemployed already are trained and even those who are not trained should not be forced to move to another community in order to get a job.
I have referred to this example before but I think it is important to repeat it over and over again. When the House of Commons committee on this bill went to Sudbury, Ontario, it was pointed out to us that in 1982 when we had a recession in this country and, as well, the nickel prices went down considerably, 10,000 people lost their jobs in Sudbury.

speechtext:
The member over there says: "Due to a Liberal Government". Mr. Speaker, that is the depth of knowledge of Conservatives. They do not realize that nickel prices are set on a world-wide basis and only to a very small extent are determined here in this country. That demonstrates why the Conservatives are at 15 per cent in the polls. They keep on making those stupid, silly comments. The more they make those stupid, silly comments, the more they go down in the polls. I encourage the member for Burlington to keep it up because if he keeps it up we will keep going up in the polls and they will keep going down.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, in Sudbury 10,000 people were laid off in 1982 due to a drop in nickel prices but because we had a solid, substantial unemployment insurance system those people were able to take care of their families, pay their rent and keep their homes during that period of time. When nickel prices went up again, also under a Liberal government, the town was restored to its economic base and many of those people were taken back on their jobs. The unemployment insurance had sustained the community during that period of time, a community which, for the most part, relies on the mining industry.
One could repeat that example in many other parts of this country, whether the community relies on the automobile industry, the forest industry, the fishing industry, the oil industry or whatever it may be. When the prices go down you have a lot of lay-offs and a lot of hardship, but unemployment insurance sees those people through that hard period.
I was also amused today at how the government and the minister, in this case, says that this bill is necessary because we must take care of the deficit and the way we must take care of the deficit is by paying for training out of the unemployment insurance program. I have to
remind the government and the House that the unemployment insurance fund was not in a deficit when the government introduced this bill. As a matter of fact, in 1988, the year before the government introduced this bill, the unemployment insurance fund had a surplus of $2.8 billion.
It is true that the total government funds were in deficit, the country was in deficit, but the unemployment insurance fund had a surplus of $2.8 billion. Of course, that is the reason why the government decided to pay for training out of the unemployment insurance fund. It saw a fund with a surplus and decided to take the surplus away from the unemployed and use it to pay for training. That was a very good objective but the wrong method of carrying it out.
The minister spoke a lot about the role of the Senate. In referring to the amendments proposed by the Senate she said: "We cannot accept the views of an unelected body". In saying that she suggests that the amendments put forward by the Senate were in some way conceived on the floor of the Senate. That is not true. The Senate held quite extensive hearings on this bill and the amendments that it put forward are to a great extent based on the views of those who appeared before it at those hearings. In other words, the amendments put forward by the Senate to this bill are amendments which have broad support in this country. They are not amendments that simply reflect the views of the unelected Senators. In this case, the unelected Senators are better expressing the views and public opinion in this country than is the government.
I must point out that in the hearings that were held by the House of Commons legislative committee on this bill, 157 of the 202 groups appearing before the House of Commons committee opposed this bill. That is an extremely high percentage of groups opposing the bill. The same thing happened in the Senate.
The minister this afternoon tried to give the impression that the premier of Newfoundland favoured this bill. I have not checked with the premier of Newfoundland. It may be that he favours more money for training, but I doubt very much if he favours paying for training out of unemployment insurance moneys. I was with the committee when it was in Newfoundland and not one witness group in Newfoundland supported this bill. I believe it was the same with the Senate. I believe it was the same with the Senate. I can assure this House and
May 7, 1990

the minister that Newfoundlanders do not support this bill.
In referring to the Senate and the fact that senators are not elected, and to who really represents the people in this country, I have to repeat again that during the election of 1988 this proposal to cut back on unemployment insurance was not part of the Conservative party platform.
As a matter of fact, when the Minister for International Trade was asked in Newfoundland whether there would be any cuts to the unemployment insurance program, he said absolutely not. He went on to say that he spoke to the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister assured him that there would be no changes or cuts to the unemployment insurance program.
Here we have a government which pretends to speak for the Canadian people but a government which did not get a mandate from the Canadian people to make cuts in the unemployment insurance program. One must recall that the government party, the Conservative party at that, only got 48 per cent of the votes of the Canadian people. The two opposition parties combined got 52 per cent of the vote.
I hate repeating this, but since the election the support for the government has declined week after week. As a matter of fact, if it keeps at it, it will be into a negative position very soon. It has dropped from 48 per cent to 15 or 16 per cent in the recent polls.
On the weekend the Prime Minister admitted that it is not over. He is right on there. One of the few times I have agreed with the Prime Minister is when he said that this drop in the polls will continue. It will continue as long as the government insists on putting before Parliament this kind of legislation for which it has no mandate.
If the Senate is so bad in its present form, as the minister and the government members pretend, then why has the government not taken steps to reform it? In the last Parliament, in 1985 or 1986, the Conservative Minister of Justice was quite angry with the Senate and he put a bill before the House to reform the Senate. But that bill sat on the Order Paper and was never moved ahead and when the session ended, the bill died. Instead of reforming the Senate, every time there was a vacancy
Government Orders
the government appointed senators, their favourite people.

speechtext: You are wrong. You are absolutely wrong.

speechtext:
I am absolutely wrong, they say. I could name a whole list. That is such a ridiculous comment it is not even worth answering.
It is true that the government has not yet filled all the vacancies, but after presenting the bill it did in the last Parliament and not proceeding with that bill, it went on to appoint Conservatives to the Senate. It has not filled all the vacancies, but it did not do one thing to reform the Senate which it now says is so bad.
I have heard some of the Conservative members in their speeches saying that these cut-backs in unemployment insurance are necessary because unemployment insurance is an incentive to laziness, that if you have an unemployment insurance system that really helps the unemployed to pay for their groceries and rent, there will be a tendency for these workers to quit their jobs or not to look for work and to just loaf around all the time.
I have to remind our Conservative friends that we have the same unemployment insurance system right across this country, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, in Ontario and in Prince Edward Island. It is the same program. Yet we have a 4.5 per cent unemployment rate in southern Ontario and a 17 per cent unemployment rate in Newfoundland. Are these Conservatives saying that unemployment insurance is an incentive to laziness in Newfoundland but not in Ontario? Is it an incentive to laziness in Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, but not in Calgary or Vancouver?
If unemployment insurance was an incentive to laziness, it would be an incentive to laziness everywhere. That is a nonsense argument. The answer to that is that some of the most progressive countries with social programs in the world have sound, substantial, unemployment insurance programs. West Germany, Japan, Scandinavian countries, France, and Great Britain all have strong unemployment insurance programs and many of them have very low unemployment rates.
Unemployment insurance is not the cause of unemployment. It is not an incentive to unemployment. People want to work. I referred to Newfoundland where the unemployment rate is around 17 per cent and the real rate is much higher than that. Many people are

May 7, 1990
Government Orders
forced to leave that province to seek work in other provinces because they want to work so much.
I already referred to this, but we have to remind ourselves over and over again that the economy of Canada is strongly based on resources and seasonal industries. When you have an economy based on resources and seasonal industries, no matter how much you want to work there will be times when you will be unemployed because of world prices for those resources or simply because it is winter.
We had an argument in Prince Edward Island as to whether the fact that a large percentage of the Prince Edward Island economy was based on the tourism industry had anything to do with unemployment in the winter. Well, anybody with any sense would know that there are fewer jobs in Prince Edward Island in the winter than there are in the summer because of the fact that the tourism industry has to close down to a certain extent. It is true that they are trying to get conventions to the island and they are trying to replace the summer tourism with other things, but nevertheless seasonal conditions have a great impact on unemployment in this country.
Although the government has condemned the Senate in this debate, I think we have to be thankful to the Senate because by its persistence the government has finally accepted some of its amendments. If the Senate had not taken the steps that it did, we would not have had the two amendments the government accepted the last time, one having to do with training people who have problems with illiteracy. This time the government has accepted three more amendments.
That is not nearly good enough, but it points to the fact that the sober second thought of the Senate has either forced or convinced the government that certain changes were necessary, and not only were they necessary but they were worth-while amendments. I repeat again that these amendments which the Senate presented were not ones they conceived in their own minds on the floor of the Senate, but were amendments which had been sent to them and suggested to them from all over the country by a large number of groups. As a matter of fact, many of them were similar to amendments we put forward in this Chamber but which were defeated by the large majority of Conservatives on the other side.
In responding to the government's arguments with respect to the Senate, the government keeps alleging that the Senate blocked this bill or that the Senate turned back this bill. The Senate did no such thing. The Senate could have, because there is a Liberal majority, defeated this bill. It did not do that. It did not defeat the bill and it did not delay the bill. As soon as it received the bill and received the message from the House of Commons, it dealt with it immediately in both cases. It had public hearings, it considered the bill. The Senate did not defeat it but made amendments to the bill; amendments which, as I said, were based on wide ranging public opinion in this country, and it sent the bill back. So it did not obstruct or defeat or turn down the bill, but simply attempted to improve the bill.
We in the opposition are willing to support the Senate's amendments, but only as a minimum. We do not think the Senate amendments go far enough. As a matter of fact, our preference was that this bill be totally withdrawn by the government and sent back to the drawing board and that it come up with something much better and much more beneficial for Canadian unemployed.
In the last Parliament the government appointed the Forget Royal Commission to study the unemployment insurance system, a commission that cost $18 million. The commission sat for more than a year and presented a report with recommendations. The government did nothing with those recommendations. These changes in Bill C-21 do not reflect the suggestions made by Mr. Forget and his commission. This is not to say that we the Liberal opposition agreed with all of Mr. Forget's proposals. We did not. The fact of the matter is that the government did not accept any of his suggestions either and Bill C-21 is contrary, as a matter of fact, to many of the recommendations made by the Forget Commission.
Furthermore, in the last Parliament, the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration studied the Forget Commission report and the unemployment insurance system and we made 71 recommendations for improvement and change in the unemployment insurance system. It was a unanimous report on all but two recommendations. It was a unanimous report on 68 recommendations by a committee with a Conservative majority and the government has not implemented any of those recommendations or suggestions. It ignored a royal commission that it set up,
May 7, 1990	COMMONS DEBATES	11071
it ignored a House of Commons committee where it had the majority of members, and it is proceeding with a bill which is opposed by social, religious, and trade union groups all over the country.
The purpose of this bill is not to help the unemployed or to reform the unemployment insurance system. The real purpose of this bill is to help the government deal with its deficit and also to harmonize its social programs with the United States as result of the free trade agreement.
In the United States, where unemployment insurance is a state matter, a state responsibility, the total amount spent on unemployment insurance is $13 billion. That is the same amount that is spent in Canada.
It is very significant that many of the changes that the government has in this bill are similar to provisions contained in the the American unemployment insurance laws. One has to admit that there are some states which have a fairly sound and substantial unemployment insurance system, but there are other states where it is a scandal for a modern, progressive country, where unemployed people must still rely on relief and charity.
The purpose of this bill is not to help the unemployed. It is not to reform the unemployment insurance system. It is not really to deal with training because, if the government really believed in training, it would not have cut the training program by 32 per cent between 1984 and 1988. The real purpose is to deal with the deficit and to harmonize our social programs with those of the United States.
In conclusion, we are willing to support, as a minimum, the amendments suggested by the Senate, but we really do not think that is the solution to the problem of the unemployed in this country. The solution is, of course, training, but it is also jobs, economic development, regional development and a better and more substantial unemployment insurance system because, no matter what, when people are without work they have to pay for the essentials of life.
This afternoon I have tried to deal with some of what I consider to be ridiculous nonsense arguments put forward by the minister. I did not deal with the questions of procedure or constitutionality with respect to the Senate.

I urge the government to listen to the people of this country. At the present time, the views of the people of this country are being expressed through the Senate and, I say, thank God for the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the many points made by my hon. friend who has just spoken. He raised some very good points.
In general, we have to be very cautious as to what is occurring in the House at this moment. I think we could make the case that we are actually in the middle of a major battle, a battle between this House and the Senate, a battle between the Prime Minister's and Privy Council offices and the duly elected members of this House, and a battle between the government and Canadian workers. I think it is fair to say that there have been a lot of casualties in these battles. We do not have many foreign correspondents in the gallery or the International Red Cross, but I think we can still make the case that casualties abound.
At the top of the list in terms of casualties on this battleground is the delicate balance of our parliamentary democracy. Tragic casualties in this process has been the balance between the rights of the majority to govern and the rights of the minority to be heard, and the balance between the responsibilities of both Chambers in this Parliament to protect and to provide a democratic legislative base.
Today, I listened with interest to the minister responsible for this legislation as she pretended to defend democracy. She read part of the motion that the government has brought forward which, once again, introduces a form of closure on debating further regulations regarding people in the fishing industry. To agree to the motion would be to agree to a form of closure in terms of debate in the House in future years. That is not what democracy is all about.
The government is asking us to agree to a motion today that asserts that only the elected House has the right to study meaningfully money bills. It is asking us to defend the rights of the elected members of this House. Yet, it is this government that has done more than

May 7, 1990
Government Orders
people could ever have imagined to diminish the rights of these same elected members time and time again.
I only have to think of those two Conservative members from Alberta who decided to do the democratic thing and represent their constituents on this important economic matter. It was not a moral issue, because I think we all recognize that, when it comes to moral issues, people ought to have the right to express freely their moral position on issues. However, when it comes to economic matters or government policy regarding taxation, surely, members of Parliament have some obligation to represent the views of their constituents.
When the member from Edmonton and the member from Calgary asked their constituents what they felt they should do in terms of the goods and services tax, 70, 80, or 85 per cent of their constituents said that they should stop the tax dead in its tracks. So, they spoke out against the tax. They said that they could not support a tax opposed by almost everybody in their constituency, everybody they knew in the country, and most Canadians by far. They could not go ahead and pass it.
What did the government do? The government that is now arguing that we must listen to the democratic voices speaking in the country and that we must emphasize the democratic basis of this institution? It kicked those members out of the caucus. They do not sit over there any more. The Prime Minister said: "You cannot represent your constituents. We do not want anything to do with democracy in this party. You are out. I do not want to see you again." So they sit with members of the opposition.
Here is the minister, shedding crocodile tears, on bended knee, pleading for democracy, when in her own caucus she supports the most undemocratic act we have seen in years.
The elected members on this side of the House, and Canadians, will not be deceived by this particular request. We know that the motion before us today will do absolutely nothing to revive or restore the health of parliamentary democracy ip (.fie country. We have seen what the government has done since it has come to office in terms of eroding what we have come to know as parliamentary democracy, our parliamentary system.
This motion will not restore the privileges of elected members to represent freely and openly their constituents' interests, unfettered by threats of closure and time allocation. We have seen something historically never witnessed before in the House. Every eight days closure has been threatened when it is averaged out over the entire term.
This motion will not restore the privileges of elected members by the dictatorial rulings of certain committee chairs. A committee chairman is sitting here today. There have been dictatorial rulings. It is not going to change that.
This motion will not restore the privileges of elected members of the House to have the opportunity to present petitions and bills on behalf of their constituents during Routine Proceedings. Day after day we have seen the government curtail Routine Proceedings. Those of us who have stacks of petitions to present on the goods and services tax are denied that right. The motion before us will not make this government responsible to this House of elected members. It will not make the government come to this House to announce to elected representatives its new programs and policies.
Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, when the government decided it was going to introduce what it thought was a great environmental plan, The Green Plan? Did it introduce it in the House of Commons, before the duly-elected members representing the people of Canada? No, it was done at a press conference some place.
It will not make the government fulfil its moral responsibility to come to the House and implement policy by legislation, instead of by administrative fiat and regulatory change, as it did when it slashed VIA Rail from existence. Was that done in the House of Commons? No, that was done in secret. It was the same kind of secrecy when the government said that it did not like the priest who was standing outside the House. This motion before us will not restore the confidence of Canadians in our parliamentary system. How could that confidence be restored when the government has ignored the pleas of Canadians to reduce interest rates? It totally ignores those calls. People are saying: "Reduce interest rates." Financiers are saying: "Reduce interest rates." Does the government listen? No, it knows best. Big government and big brother knows best.
How could the confidence in the government be restored when it has ignored the pleas of Canadians to provide leadership on the environment? When it has ignored the pleas to withdraw regressive tax programs? And when it has ignored the pleas from fishermen, farmers and those living in the regions of Canada?
The motion before us will do nothing to restore the trust that Canadians once had in their government. I must say that it is no coincidence that since the government launched its offences against parliamentary democracy, there has been a tragic increase in intolerance, bitterness and cynicism toward government in the coun-
Government Orders
try. It is as though the people have lost faith in their government.
Today's skirmish is against the Senate. I want to refer to the Senate, not to the other place. Let us call a spade a spade. We are talking about an impasse with the Senate. The message before us a missile against the Senate. The Prime Minister and the rest of his war room are trying to remove the rights of the Senate to oppose, to amend, or to improve legislation, just as they have removed the rights of elected members in the House of Commons.
Unfortunately, there are many civilian casualties in this battle, including thousands of Canadians in depressed regions who for four months have been deprived of unemployment insurance benefits to which they are entitled, because the government has repeatedly refused to separate the variable entrance rate component of this legislation and give it the rapid passage that we have offered. They would rather see Canadian workers in the maritimes, rural Canada, and in the west and north live in poverty than admit that the Senate has the constitutional right to study Bill C-21.
Other casualties include Canadian mothers whose rights to maternity benefit equalities were fought for in the courts and were won. These rights are now held hostage in the battle over cuts to unemployment insurance that have nothing to do with maternity benefits.
I ask the members opposite to lay down their arms for a brief while during this debate and take the opportunity to reflect on how we arrived at this very unhappy situation. If you look back over the last year and a half, Mr. Speaker, you will see a number of events that lead us to today's debate. In the cold autumn of 1988 the Conservatives took the country to the polls on an election that became a one issue campaign, free trade. Most Canadians were opposed to free trade on November 21. Some New Democrats say that is why the government lost the moral right to impose the trade deal. The view of democracy did not suit this Prime Minister and free trade was forced through the House in unprecedented time through the use of closure at every single stage.
I acknowledge that many Canadians voted for the free trade agreement, but they did so believing that they had a commitment from the Conservatives to provide training and adjustment programs. They trusted that the government would assist those who would inevitably lose their jobs as a result of this realignment of our economy.

Some Canadians voted for free trade believing promises that the Conservatives stated again and again; that our social programs would not be affected, that they would not be harmonized with the harsher, stingier programs offered to American workers.
Five months after the Conservatives were democratically elected to fulfil these commitments they instead turned against Canadian democracy. They did so by abrogating their election commitment to training programs and introduced Bill C-21, which is what we are talking about today, which removes any federal government contribution to training.
Think of the federal dollars that go into assisting lawyers to be trained. Thousands and thousands of dollars from the general treasury go to help lawyers get training. Why not the same for machinists? Why treat certain kinds of people differently in terms of the training and education they receive?
The government also turned against Canadian democracy by abrogating its election commitment to maintain social programs, by introducing Bill C-21, which harmonizes our unemployment insurance program more closely with that of the United States program.
It also denies the government's responsibility to help unemployed Canadians, even though they lost their jobs as a result of the government policy to push consumer interest rates up past 15 per cent and unemployment to more than a million people, to say nothing about the cuts to student programs for the summer. Many students are trying to earn money for their own education and training options.
Bill C-21 is a massive policy change in that it destroys an institutionalized and complexly woven social security net in our country. No attempt was ever made to hide the fact that the Conservatives planned for months before the election to destroy this program and some suggest it might have even been part of the discussions around the free trade deal.
Was it a democratic act to make specific commitments during an election campaign and then introduce a long-planned strategy that was the very opposite of those commitments? Obviously not. Was it not an act against democracy when the government forced closure
after only five hours of debate on this very sinister legislation? Was it a service to free and open democracy to severely restrict hearings on this bill? Was democracy helped when almost one-third of those groups who wished to appear were denied an opportunity to express their concerns, or when the testimony, including crossexamination, was restricted to less than half an hour? Was it remotely democratic to listen to witnesses and then ignore their testimony? The vast majority, 157 of 202 witnesses strongly opposed this bill, yet their opinions counted for nothing.
When the minister of the Crown responsible for the bill finally appeared before the committee, was it a democratic act to give members of this House less than one hour of questioning time with the minister? Were the democratic privileges of this House and the rights of its members aided when time allocation was imposed at both report stage and third reading stage? No, they were not. Was it a democratic act when members were denied even the opportunity to explain the proposed amendments and present short arguments as to why they should be adopted?
It was an affront to democracy for the government to blithely ignore the mandate it was given to provide training programs and to protect social programs. I suggest that it was an affront to parliamentary democracy for the government to blithely ignore the rights of members to debate the principles of the bill, to engage in meaningful committee review, and to offer proposed changes.
I must say that Canadians knew what was going on. They saw the House was being denied its historic rights in a free and democratic society. They saw the rubber stamp that has now become a symbol of Conservative democracy. They then turned to the Senate. I know many Canadian political activists were surprised to find themselves knocking on the Senate door asking Senators to do the work that members of the House had been prevented from doing. I know many people had to re-examine their view of the Senate. New Democrats were among those who looked again at the role of the Senate.

New Democrats watched intently the assault on democracy which took place last year. We exercised our democratic rights within our own party and voted at our December convention to change our party policy on the Senate. Whereas once we were satisfied that the Senate had to be abolished, and that was it, we are now in the process of looking at a variety of options to provide and promote better regional representation in the Parliament of Canada, including but not limited to, proportional representation, an elected Senate, and other options.
New Democrats who voted for that position are ordinary Canadians who were looking at what this government has done to parliamentary democracy in our country, Canadians who want protection from the kind of totalitarian behaviour we have seen with this Conservative government.
New Democrats were among those who went to the Senate and requested that it block the imposition of Bill C-21. Through their labour councils, social councils, churches and women's groups, they asked the Senate to protect the unemployment insurance program that their fathers and mothers and fellow social democrats had fought so hard to establish. These ordinary New Democrats and ordinary Canadians generally, told the Senate of the importance of maintaining a healthy unemployment insurance program, of the need for government to play a role in training programs, of the responsibility of government toward unemployed workers.
Unfortunately, the Senate is not full of ordinary New Democrats or ordinary Canadians. It obviously did not understand the arguments that were put before it. Instead of amending Bill C-21 in a way which would ensure the integrity of our Canadian unemployment insurance plan, the Senate offered a few minor improvements to a very bad piece of legislation.
I remember seeing Liberal Senators on television with tears in their eyes, who were so emotional at the stories they were hearing that they could not speak. Did they really do anything to change that bill? Did they stop the legislation? Did they suggest major changes? No. Did they answer the call when witness after witness came to them and pleaded for the same changes to Bill C-21? Surely not. No witness asked for the version of Bill C-21 which the Senate voted to send back to this House. It is

The point I want to make is that the Senate failed Canadians. When Canadians made their case before the Senate committee hearings, obviously the Senate did not hear those cases. They ignored the pleas being put forward by individuals and groups across the country.
I do not know that we should be surprised at that. When you look at the Senate, as it will be at least until June 23, it was the Liberals who five times between 1975 and 1985 cut back the unemployment insurance program. The Liberals removed the federal responsibility for unemployment insurance, except for regionally extended benefits. The Liberals developed the policy now implemented by the Conservative government that high unemployment is an acceptable price for stabilized prices.
Clearly, the Liberal Senators were not interested in helping Canadian workers. Liberal Senators were not interested in protecting a program which had been so undemocratically removed. Clearly, they were taking Canadians down the Senate path, promising hearings, hinting at a meaningful review, but in the end doing virtually nothing.
All along, the Liberal Senate only seemed to be interested in a showdown with the House of Commons. It chose to hold this showdown over a few relatively insignificant improvements to a very flawed bill. So we are back to the old battle between this House and the Senate. During the last debate on this issue this House agreed to include basic skills and literacy training among the many types of training offered using unemployment insurance funds.
We agreed to provide greater detail and annual development uses, all those plans which would show how the government intended to use the money provided under the UI Act.
Finally, we agreed that any proposed repeal of the system of UI benefits for self-employed fishermen would require parliamentary approval.
With the motion before us now we have decided to strengthen our commitments made during the last debate and make additional changes to the legislation.
In particular, as members of this House know, we have agreed to change an aspect of the rules affecting people who quit their jobs without just cause.
The Senate asked for lighter penalties for those people. It stated that we were being too hard on those people who quit, that they should not have to wait as long for UI benefits. It asked for change in two areas and we have agreed to one, because this is a compromise that does not weaken our emphasis on workers who quit jobs, an important principle behind this whole bill. We also understand, even if we do not share, the Senate's
Government Orders
concerns regarding fishermen's benefits. These benefits are safe.
As I noted, the government has already agreed to eliminate a provision in the current Unemployment Insurance Act which would have allowed a government to eliminate these benefits by proclamation. This provision was originally placed there by a Liberal regime.
The government, in this motion, has modified Senate recommendation 8 to provide for a formal review process for any proposed changes to UI regulations pertaining to fishing benefits. We can agree that such a review is appropriate, but we firmly believe that this review process must be conducted in the House of Commons, and not in the Senate.
The government has made these concessions in a spirit of conciliation. We have not asked for, nor provoked, the current situation. It is disappointing that it is only this House and this government which has shown a willingness to compromise on this bill. We cannot go further without making fundamental changes which would undermine the basic principles of the bill that we originally brought forward.
One of those basic principles forms the second theme in this debate, the need to support and reaffirm our concept that the benefits that will flow from this bill will flow for training and for workers.
Bill C-21 will allow the government to implement the labour force development strategy, which provides many improvements to Canada's labour market polices and to its unemployment insurance program. These improvements are part of a well planned strategy to meet the challenges of a world economy which is being driven by scientific and technological change. Mr. Speaker, we cannot stand still.
Advances in science and technology have affected an extremely wide range of jobs. Let us use one simple example. Consider the impact of computers whether it be in the factory, in the store, on the farm or anywhere. Not only do they affect the way jobs are done, but they affect the skills that are required to do those jobs. That is the reason why no one argues about the importance of training and education.
Last year, the Conference Board of Canada found that two out of every three Canadian firms reported difficulties with employees who were illiterate and unable to carry out their assigned work. In fact, half of all Cana-

dian firms have trouble finding workers with the appropriate skills.
Someone has said that the economic race between industrialized nations is a competition not between industries but between various educational systems. To make use of modern technology, as we must do, requires a modern, trained workforce. We need to have it built on a solid educational system linked with training and development that will meet the changing needs as they arise.
We will have to improve the training available to our workers. Otherwise, we will not be able to generate the kind of wealth that this country needs, if we are going to have the programs that Canadians want. Surely by now, we recognize that most of that training will have to be done by the private sector.
Employers benefit greatly from a well trained staff. They have the responsibility to train their employees, and to ensure that the skills are kept current. While we apparently understand that, it is generally agreed the one area which Canada must improve is industrial private sector training.
We, in government, believe it is necessary to promote a training culture in Canadian business. We know that the private sector must do its share in bringing about the kinds of skills development on which it all depends.
One major goal of the labour force development strategy is to bring the training efforts of our own private sector up to levels which match those of other countries. The bill now before us is directly related to that goal. It will make $230 million available to increase training by the private sector, where it needs to be. That money will be invested in projects which will, in turn, trigger even more investment by the private sector.
We believe the labour force development strategy can help lead to a $1.5 billion additional expenditure by the private sector over the next four years. At that level, which we are trying to achieve, on a per capita basis the private sector training in Ggpttda will just match that of the United States. For that to happen a strategy is necessary. That is why we introduced Bill C-21 in the first place.
In a very real sense, what we have before us is enabling legislation. Changing the Unemployment Insurance Act is only a part of what we have to do. In making the changes we are talking about, it provides both the legislative basis and the financial means to pursue one of the most critical goals facing any nation today, the development of a work-force which will remain competitive in world markets and ensure prosperity at home.
This legislation is a kind of ignition key for the labour force strategy. It will address some of our most pressing problems. We have a mandate in this Parliament, as in any Parliament, to improve training and adjustment programs to bring about better training and a fairer system of unemployment insurance.
Let me remind the House that Bill C 21 will increase the federal funding available for labour force development by some 45 per cent. That is one of the purposes. Without this support, tens of thousands of Canadians may not receive the assistance and training they need to change and adapt to a new labour market and will not become productive members of that labour market.
The labour force strategy is also designed to reach those Canadian workers who most need assistance. It is about the young, the 30 per cent who have dropped out of school, who need access to better entry level type jobs. It is about women, native people, visible minorities, and the disabled, all of those who can benefit from inclusion in an equitable human resource planning concept. It is about older Canadians who need training to cope with changing job demands. They are not getting enough training now. We have to make some changes in direction. I think the strategy will clear away some obstacles. We need human resource planning, more co-operative education, and better and more apprenticeship training.
The successful nation has to have significant training opportunities for its youth, the elderly and for those people who are going to change their jobs several times during their lifetime. We have to be part of that changing work-force strategy. We think a more focused training and career development program can help unleash a great untapped pool of talent and skill, but it can only happen if we are prepared to plan for and work towards it.

We need to plan together at various levels so that we can adjust our market forces, let people have the training they need to be useful members and have the pride of having a good and valuable job. That is why I support this legislation. I want that kind of opportunity for the people of this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am pleased to rise in support of the motion by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. In the throne speech last year this government set out its intention to build a strong economy that was fully competitive among the world's trading nations.
We further announced our intention to amend the unemployment insurance program to improve its effectiveness and its fairness. This would result in more resources being directed towards active training, leading
May 7, 1990

to more opportunities and a more productive, experienced workforce.
At this point I want to ask the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence if I could have his attention for just a moment because I want to give him a little bit of history. When I came to this Parliament in 1972, we had before us in 1973, amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. At that time, if the minister overran his allotment in the Estimates by $400 million, he had to come before Parliament and ask for an extra allotment. In 1973, that figure was doubled, from $400 million to $800 million. In 1974, we took the lid off altogether.
Your comments about stealing money from the unemployment insurance account to pay for training is not valid. The statute and information states that if an unemployed worker needs money and there is nothing in the fund, it comes automatically from the general revenue fund. You should remember that because you are not being valid in your comments.
We were elected in 1984 and re-elected in 1988 with a mandate that includes controlling federal spending in order to maintain economic stability, continued growth, and to prepare Canadians for participation in the international economy of a wide new world.
We will help meet that mandate through Bill C-21. It sets in place a human resource strategy for the 1990s that will address the imperatives of the modern economy. Unlike the Senate, which is prepared to add at least $1.75 billion annually to the deficit, we will do so in co-operation with the private sector without expanding our debt.
The individual worker is still the most vital part of any workplace. It is in this regard that Canada faces its greatest challenge. In 1989, the world competitive scoreboard ranked Canada well down on the list with respect to managerial talent, R and D, personnel and skilled labour.
The Conference Board of Canada last year found that two out of every three Canadian firms reported difficulties with employees who were illiterate and who were unable to carry out their assigned tasks.
Government Orders
In fact the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre estimated that more than 600,000 job vacancies go unfilled in Canada despite the relatively high unemployment in many areas because workers do not measure up to the skill demands in the job.
This is a comprehensive program that we have involving all parts of our educational and training system. We have had to re-examine our whole approach to developing our human resources in this country, from basic education through to skills training, to labour market programs on adjustment and on unemployment insurance. This is now taking place.
The Prime Minister has called for a national debate on education in Canada and its relationship to economic productivity and competitiveness. He has further called for discussions with provincial ministers of education on the mechanism to set up a task force on resource development.
The national initiative on education complements what we are doing with Bill C-21, which amends the UI Act. It allows for a 45 per cent increase in funding for labour force development and gives life to the Labour Force Development Strategy. This strategy is to fulfil two objectives: first, to increase the quality of training and skills development in Canada with a greater commitment on the part of the private sector and, second, to increase the quality of training so that it is more relevant, hands on and committed to excellence.
Canadian industry spends less than one-half of the amount that U.S. firms spend on training, which is a fraction of what other countries such as Japan spend. Bill C-21 makes $230 million available to increased training by the private sector, which is leverage money that will trigger an estimated $1.5 billion in addition to investment and training over the next four years. Our goal is to create a training culture where employees and companies practise skills development on an ongoing basis. That means working in partnership with community colleges and the provincial government to provide quality training that is relevant and market oriented.
The Labour Force Development Strategy is designed to reach those workers who most need assistance. It is about young people, the 30 per cent who have dropped out of school and have trouble accessing the labour

Government Orders
market. When Bill C-21 is passed we will be dedicating $100 million for the purpose of setting up new entry level training programs primarily directed at young people. This will supplement existing programs such as apprenticeship which, by the way, will be examined in consultation with industry and the provinces to accommodate the growing demand for skills in the service sector.
Moreover, we will be quadrupling federal expenditures on co-operative education, a popular program among young people which is growing in demand. Our intention is to expand this program into the high schools.
Unemployed workers will see more assistance to help them get into the workforce. The passage of Bill C-21 will enable the federal government to spend $350 million a year to reach an additional 60,000 UI recipients this year. We are also aiming to help those Canadians who are on social assistance and who have been left behind. Bill C-21 will see $50 million added to the current training and other employment programs which have been operating in co-operation with the provinces since 1986.
I do not need to remind the House that each success means another pay cheque for families in the local community, as well as the satisfaction of a worker who is able to look ahead to future opportunities. Let me add also that Bill C-21 will allow for increased training allowances to bring them up to today's standard of living.
We have difficulties with older workers. Older workers will also receive more assistance. The bill has earmarked $40 million to encourage employers to hire and retain older workers who would otherwise lose their jobs. About $50 million is intended for skills and training education upgrading to be conducted through Section 26 of the UI Act. Natives, women, visible minorities, the disabled-all those who are often denied their full place in the workforce-need the benefits that will come from a better equity based human resource planning. More focused training and career development can tap a great pool of talent and skill, but that can only happen by the building of networks and organizations involved in training, business associations, unions, vocational schools, community colleges, and others. We need to plan together at various levels; most importantly at the local level.
These are the goals of the policy on which Bill C-21 is based.
The status quo is no longer acceptable for Canada. Quite simply, to stand still is to fall back.
That is the big picture, but the human side is quite simple. Canadians want to work. They want to own homes. They want to raise families. They want their children to get an education and have jobs, and they want to provide for a secure retirement of their own. Wanting these things, Canadians expect and indeed deserve the kind of help this legislation will provide.
Canadians understand the government's efforts to make the UI a more constructive, pro-active program. Recent polls show a strong majority of Canadians support the idea of using UI funds to train unemployed people so that they find better jobs and find them sooner.
We have an opinion from the Department of Justice that we are quite legal in using the funds in this way. Two Decima polls and an Environics study found that approximately two-thirds of Canadians supported the government's plan to shift a percentage of UI funds to job training through Bill C-21. It is obvious, as well, that Canadians support the bill's measures to ensure the UI system is being used as efficiently and as effectively as possible.
This general support is also reflected by opinion makers in the media and elsewhere.
Canada has one of the most generous UI systems in the industrialized world. Fine tuning that system to make it more efficient and constructive has been generally seen in the media for what it is. What we are doing has received positive comment from across the country.

Here is one from the Saint-John Evening Times Globe. The editorialist writes that "to delay enactment-would hurt, not help the unemployed". This was written in November and the hurt continues.
From the Financial Post: "the Senate delay has forced new UI applicants to wait an additional four weeks" and "the delay also ignores the urgency of getting more job training and retraining programs up and running".
The Woodstock Daily Sentinel Review:

That is a tragedy. The Regina Leader Post:
The proposed changes-are clearly designed to make the unemployment safety net more sensitive to the job market.
The Calgary Herald:
The federal government has set out to turn UI into what it is supposed to be, an insurance policy for the genuinely unemployed job seeker.
Finally, from the Vancouver Sun:
The Senate committee members didn't have a single question for Barbara McDougall when she gave them the opportunity to quiz her about the bill. That shows that they have run out of excuses for stalling it.
There you are, Mr. Speaker. That is what many members of the media said about the stalling of this bill. I noticed as well that members opposite have quoted Global Economics, a think-tank in this country. Members quoted these studies when we travelled with the committee across the country.
It was rather strange that when Global Economics representative, Mr. Patrick O'Grady, appeared before the Senate committee, he said: "I believe that Bill C-21 will make the UI system better and it ought to be passed". These are the very people that the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace talked about, and the study they produced which said that we were all wrong. Yet, when the people who wrote that report came before the
Government Orders
committee, he told them that it would improve the bill and they should pass it.
Canadians are also very aware of the financial implications of continuing to play games with this important legislation.

If the government accepts the Senate amendments $1.75 billion will be added to the deficit; $450 million is at stake for maternity, parental and sickness benefits; and $45 million is being risked by the Senate for self-employed entrepreneurship and mobility assistance.
Members talk about the small village here and the small village there. We would all like to go back and retire in a small village. Members can go to Cambridge and ask the hon. member for Cambridge how many Newfoundlanders reside there. He will say that half the community comes from Newfoundland.
In and around the Hamilton area, there are all kinds of people from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. They came to where the jobs were to make some money and perhaps retire. We have to balance this thing. People move to where the jobs are. We are not going to move the Steel Company of Canada to Lockeport, Nova Scotia.

deficit reduction in 1990-91.
That is the key issue behind this motion. The paramount fiscal policy objectives of this government is to get the public debt under control through deficit reduction.
Let me explain how this will happen. The UI program has been financed on a tripartite basis from employer to employee premiums and from general government revenues raised by taxation and borrowing.
The proportion of benefits paid by general government revenues has varied over the years. For example, in 1989 the government paid out an estimated $2.9 billion in unemployment insurance expenditures out of a total of $12.6 billion. This was used to finance extended benefits, clients taking training, or benefits for self-employed fishermen in excess of premiums they pay. However, after Bill C-21 is passed all the UI expenditures will be financed by premiums.
